title: The Illusion of Robustness: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Prediction Flips
hook: A model's accuracy barely budges when you paste in random gibberish — but under the hood, a chunk of its individual answers silently flip, some right to wrong, some wrong to right.
key_points: Prepending task-irrelevant context — even meaningless pseudo-word prefixes — barely changes aggregate accuracy on benchmarks.
But it flips individual predictions on a subset of examples: hurting some, helping others, so the net score looks stable.
This two-sided instability holds consistently across many models and datasets, though which examples flip is model-specific.
The instability's size is modulated by context type, context length, test-time compute, and how developed the model is.
Aggregate accuracy conceals real per-example tail risk — the authors argue benchmarks need per-example reliability checks too.
content_html: State-of-the-art LLMs often look robust to irrelevant context: paste a long, unrelated passage in front of a benchmark question, and overall accuracy barely moves. Zhang, Koyejo, and Yang show that stability is an illusion at the level of individual examples. Underneath a flat aggregate score, a real slice of predictions flip — some newly wrong, some newly right.
extra_html: The effect shows up even with pseudo-words — strings formed by randomly combining characters, carrying no real meaning at all — prepended to the input. It's consistent across a wide range of models and datasets, though which specific examples flip is largely model-specific, not a shared "hard set." The authors trace the size of the effect to four factors: what kind of context is prepended, how long it is, how much test-time compute the model gets to use, and where the model sits in its development lifecycle. The upshot is a blind spot in how models get evaluated: aggregate accuracy can look rock-solid while concealing context-induced tail risk that only per-example reliability checks would catch. Yanzhe Zhang, Sanmi Koyejo, and Diyi Yang, arXiv 2026 (arxiv.org/abs/2607.12963).

related.title: Beyond Static Leaderboards for Agents
related.hook: Topping an agent leaderboard doesn't mean it'll work when deployed: aggregate-score rankings don't transfer out-of-distribution. Rank by predictive validity instead.

related.title: When Your Top Feature Makes Predictions Worse
related.hook: A feature can top your model's importance ranking and still hurt accuracy. The only way to be sure it helps: delete it, retrain, and compare on held-out data.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'aggregate stability' hide, according to this paper?
flashcards.back_html: Significant per-example instability — task-irrelevant context can flip a model's answer on individual questions even while overall accuracy barely moves.

flashcards.prompt: What kind of context can flip individual predictions, per the authors?

choices.text: Even semantically meaningless pseudo-word prefixes, formed from random characters
Only context that's topically related to the question

flashcards.explanation_html: The effect shows up even with nonsense text — it's not about meaningful distraction, just the presence of irrelevant context.

flashcards.prompt: Is the flipping effect one-directional — does irrelevant context always hurt accuracy?
flashcards.back_html: No — it's two-sided: some examples get worse, others get better, so the net aggregate score can look almost unchanged despite real underlying instability.

flashcards.prompt: What factors modulate how much of this instability shows up?

choices.text: Context type, context length, test-time compute, and model development stage
Only the size of the model in parameters

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors show the effect isn't fixed — it scales with these four factors, all measurable by practitioners.
